Here is the itemized extraction from William Sanday and Arthur C. Headlam's A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans (1895) covering the requested analytical criteria for all 12 B001 items.
1. B001-1: Romans 4:3 / Genesis 15:6
Locator / Citation: Pages 99, 101, 102
1
unfold_less
2
3
.
Discusses a Competing Textual Form: On page 99, the authors note that Origen suggested Paul originally wrote Ἀβράμ (matching the Hebrew of Gen 15), but that Gentile scribes substituted Ἀβραάμ
1
. The authors express their preference that Paul had the established name Ἀβραάμ in mind throughout
1
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar / Patristic Exegesis: On page 101, the authors refute Euthymius-Zigabenus's comment (δίκαιον ποιῆσαι), stating that the evidence is decisive that δικαιοῦν means "to declare righteous as a judge" rather than "to make righteous"
2
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation & Comparative Exegesis: On page 102, the authors compare Paul and James's use of Genesis 15:6, noting that while James appeals to a later incident (the offering of Isaac in Gen 22) to argue for works, Paul keeps more strictly to Genesis 15:6 (which speaks only of faith) and employs a searching exegesis confirmed by personal spiritual experience
3
.
2. B001-2: Romans 9:25 / Hosea 2:23 [LXX 2:25]
Locator / Citation: Page 264
4
.
Discusses a Competing Textual Form: The authors note that the Septuagint reads ἐλεήσω τὴν οὐκ ἠλεημένην, but Codex Vaticanus (B) substitutes ἀγαπήσω τὴν οὐκ ἠγαπημένην
4
. They observe that Paul used a text containing the reading of the Vatican MS, which "can hardly have been altered to harmonize with him"
4
. They contrast this with 1 Peter 2:10, which uses the majority LXX reading οἱ οὐκ ἠλεημένοι, νῦν δὲ ἐλεηθέντες
4
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation & Oral/Liturgical Transmission: The authors state that Paul inverts the order of the clauses so that τὸν οὐ λαόν μου comes first to suit the Gentiles, and substitutes καλέσω for ἐρῶ because καλέσω "naturally crept in from the ἐκάλεσεν of the previous verse"
4
. They also note that a habit had probably arisen in the early Church of quoting passages to prove the calling of the Gentiles, forming commonplaces that were later collected in written testimonia
4
.
3. B001-3: Romans 9:26 / Hosea 1:10 [LXX 2:1]
Locator / Citation: Page 264
4
.
Expresses Uncertainty & Allows Authorial Adaptation: The authors point out that the only difference between Paul's quotation and the Septuagint is his insertion of ἐκεῖ (ἐκεῖ κληθήσονται υἱοὶ θεοῦ ζῶντος), noting that "this insertion seems to emphasize the idea of the place, and it is somewhat difficult to understand what place is intended"
4
.
Acknowledges Competing Interpretations:
Palestinian / Jewish Eschatology: If original, ἐκεῖ refers to Palestine/Jerusalem and the gathering of nations there in a Messianic kingdom, showing that Paul "is often strongly influenced by the language and even the ideas of Jewish eschatology"
4
.
Universal Interpretation: If neglecting the original context, ἐκεῖ refers spiritually to "the whole world" wherever Gentiles suffer reproach
4
.
4. B001-4: Romans 10:11 / Isaiah 28:16
Locator / Citation: Page 290
5
.
Allows Authorial Adaptation: The authors observe that Paul re-quotes Isaiah 28:16 (previously cited in Rom 9:33) "with the addition of πᾶς to bring out the point on which emphasis is to be laid," namely the universal character of Gospel salvation for both Jew and Gentile
5
.
5. B001-5: Romans 10:13 / Joel 2:32 [LXX 3:5]
Locator / Citation: Page 291
6
.
Notes Hebrew / Greek Agreement: The authors note that Paul's quotation agrees verbatim with both the Septuagint and the Hebrew texts
6
.
Allows Re-application / Transfer of Old Testament Title: The authors state that the OT formula for calling on Jehovah (ἐπικαλεῖσθαι τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου) is transferred christologically by Paul to Jesus Christ (Κύριος), converting a prophetic description of the "day of the Lord" into a designation for Christian worshippers
6
. They cite A. Seeberg's treatise Die Anbetung des Herrn bei Paulus regarding prayer to Christ
6
.
6. B001-6: Romans 11:34 / Isaiah 40:13
Locator / Citation: Page 340
7
.
Disagrees with Other Scholars: The authors explicitly refute "many commentators" (specifically citing Canon Liddon) who attempted to interpret the doxological prepositions in verse 36 (ἐξ αὐτοῦ, διʼ αὐτοῦ, εἰς αὐτόν) as references to the distinct persons of the Trinity
7
. Sanday and Headlam state that "(1) the prepositions do not suit this interpretation... (2) The whole argument refers to a different line of thought," addressing the Godhead as a whole
7
.
7. B001-7: Romans 15:12 / Isaiah 11:10
Locator / Citation: Page 399
8
.
Notes Hebrew / Greek Ambiguity & Paraphrase: The authors note that Paul's quotation follows the Septuagint, "which is only a paraphrase of the Hebrew"
8
. They contrast the LXX (ὁ ἀνιστάμενος ἄρχειν ἐθνῶν, ἐπʼ αὐτῷ ἔθνη ἐλπιοῦσιν) with the literal Hebrew MT ("which standeth for an ensign of the peoples, unto him shall the Gentiles seek")
8
.
Disagrees with Another Scholar: The authors refute F. C. Baur's objection to the genuineness of Romans 15:1–13 (which claimed calling Christ a "minister of circumcision" in v. 8 was an impossible concession to Jewish Christians)
8
. They argue that Jewish priority and the fulfillment of covenant promises are fundamental to Paul's theology throughout Romans
8
.

Both St. Paul and St. James treat at some length of the history of Abraham; they both quote the same verse, Gen. xv. 6, as the salient characterization of that history; and they draw from it the conclusion—St. Paul that a man is accounted righteous πίστει χωρὶς ἔργων (Rom, iii. 28 ; cf. iv. 1--8), St. James as expressly, that he is accounted righteous ἐξ ἔργων καὶ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως μόνον (Jas. li. 24).
